objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Context Standard (LCS) governs how the contextual environment within which Liability may become relevant is identified, bounded, structured, documented, and maintained so that subsequent Liability governance occurs within an explicit and sufficiently defined context.
objects.coreQuestion: Within what context can Liability meaningfully exist and become governable?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Object Standard (LOS) governs how the specific matter in relation to which Liability is being considered is identified, formed, bounded, distinguished, represented, and maintained as a stable governed Liability Object before any Liability Basis, Liability Relationship, Liability Condition, Liability Connection, or Liability Determination is established.
objects.coreQuestion: What exactly is the governed matter in relation to which Liability is being considered?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Basis Standard (LBS) governs how the basis upon which Liability may potentially exist in relation to a Governed Liability Object is identified, classified, qualified, associated, and maintained so that subsequent Liability governance proceeds from an explicit and traceable Liability Basis rather than from consequence, assertion, assumption, responsibility, Harm, Loss, Damage, or perceived wrongdoing alone.
objects.coreQuestion: On what governed basis can Liability potentially exist?
Who or what participates in the potential Liability structure, and what Liability-relevant relationships exist between them?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Conditions Standard (LCOS) governs how the conditions relevant to potential Liability under an applicable Governed Liability Basis are identified, structured, classified, represented, evaluated as governed condition states, and maintained so that subsequent Liability governance can determine whether the required conditional structure exists for Liability-Relevant Connection and later Liability Determination.
objects.coreQuestion: What conditions must exist, fail, change, or be satisfied for potential Liability to proceed toward determination under the applicable Liability Basis?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Connection Standard (LCNS) governs how Liability-relevant connections among Liability Subjects, Governed Liability Objects, Governed Liability Conditions, conduct, events, states, actions, omissions, relationships, consequences, and other materially relevant inputs are identified, structured, traced, qualified, and represented before Liability Determination.
objects.coreQuestion: What sufficiently governed connection exists between the relevant Liability Subject, Liability Object, conditions, conduct, and other Liability-relevant inputs?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Determination Standard (LDS) governs how sufficiently established Liability Context, Liability Object, Liability Basis, Liability Relationships, Liability Conditions, and Liability-Relevant Connections are brought together, evaluated, reasoned over, and transformed into an explicit governed Liability Determination State.
objects.coreQuestion: Can Liability legitimately attach and be determined to exist on the established governed basis?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Scope & Allocation Standard (LSAS) governs how established Liability is bounded in extent and distributed across relevant Liability Subjects and Liability Relationships after Liability has been determined to attach.
objects.coreQuestion: For what and to what extent does established Liability apply, and how is that Liability distributed where multiple Liability relationships exist?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability State & Change Standard (LSCS) is the LIGA™ Parent Standard governing the current state of established Liability and the conditions, events, decisions, evidence, authority, and transitions through which that state may legitimately change over time.
objects.coreQuestion: What is the current governed state of Liability, and how may that state legitimately change?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Transfer & Recourse Standard (LTRS) is the LIGA™ Parent Standard for governing how established Liability, Liability-related obligations, Liability consequences, economic burdens, performance responsibilities, recovery rights, contribution rights, indemnification structures, insurance-related effects, succession effects, and other secondary Liability relationships may move, be shared, redistributed, recovered, or otherwise create governed relationships beyond the original Liability structure.
objects.coreQuestion: How may Liability or its consequences move, be shared, redistributed, recovered, succeeded, or create secondary Liability Relationships?
“Under what governed conditions may active Liability be resolved, satisfied, discharged, extinguished, or otherwise cease requiring active performance or governance?”

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Liability Continuity & Finality Standard (LCFS) governs the continuity, historical reconstructability, Re-entry, and legitimate Finality of Liability throughout and beyond its active governance lifecycle.
objects.coreQuestion: How must Liability remain continuous and reconstructable, when may a Liability Relationship or Liability Network legitimately reach finality, and under what conditions must governed re-entry occur?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Prediction Basis Standard (PBAS) governs the identification, inclusion, exclusion, source relationship, relevance, sufficiency, contextualization, and traceability of the information, data, observations, evidence references, signals, and other materially relevant informational elements that legitimately form the basis upon which a governed prediction is constructed.
objects.coreQuestion: What information, data, observations, evidence references, and signals legitimately form the basis of the prediction?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Prediction Assumption Standard (PAS) defines the governance conditions under which assumptions supporting a prediction are identified, expressed, bounded, associated with their dependencies, assessed for sensitivity and materiality, monitored for change, and preserved as part of the governed predictive state.
objects.coreQuestion: What assumptions must hold for the prediction and its stated probability, confidence, feasibility, or expected outcome to remain meaningful?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Prediction Formation Standard (PFOS) defines the governance conditions under which a governed Prediction Object and Purpose, documented Prediction Methodology, governed Prediction Basis, governed Predictive Assumptions, and applicable predictive conditions are transformed into a specific Governed Prediction.
objects.coreQuestion: How are methodology, Prediction Basis, assumptions, and applicable conditions transformed into a specific governed prediction?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Prediction Probability & Uncertainty Standard (PPUS) defines the governance conditions under which probability, uncertainty, confidence, ranges, intervals, conditionality, distributional representation, and related predictive qualification are associated with a Governed Prediction without overstating what the prediction actually establishes.
objects.coreQuestion: How should probability, uncertainty, confidence, ranges, and conditionality be represented without overstating what the prediction actually establishes?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Prediction Feasibility Standard (PFES) defines the governance conditions under which a Governed Prediction is assessed to determine whether the predicted outcome is realistically achievable under its stated assumptions, constraints, Prediction Horizon, Prediction Basis, applicable operational conditions, and relevant dependencies.
objects.coreQuestion: Is the predicted outcome realistically achievable under the stated assumptions, constraints, time horizon, Prediction Basis, and relevant conditions?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Collective Prediction Governance Standard (CPGS) defines the governance conditions under which predictions originating from multiple participants, models, agents, institutions, markets, forecasting mechanisms, or other predictive sources may be combined, aggregated, interpreted, represented, and relied upon as a legitimate collective prediction.
objects.coreQuestion: Under what conditions may predictions originating from multiple participants, models, agents, markets, or forecasting mechanisms be combined and represented as a legitimate collective prediction?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Prediction Communication & Reliance Standard (PCRS) defines the governance conditions under which a Governed Prediction may be communicated, represented, interpreted, distributed, contextualized, and relied upon without exceeding what its methodology, Prediction Basis, assumptions, Probability & Uncertainty, feasibility, intended purpose, Predictive Boundary, Prediction Horizon, and applicable governance qualifications legitimately support.
objects.coreQuestion: How may a prediction be communicated, interpreted, and relied upon without exceeding what its methodology, uncertainty, feasibility, intended purpose, and governed conditions legitimately support?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Prediction Monitoring & Revision Standard (PMRS) governs how a Governed Prediction is monitored after formation and use, how material changes in its Prediction Basis, assumptions, conditions, environment, probability structure, feasibility, interpretation context, or operational relevance are identified, and how the prediction is reviewed, revised, superseded, withdrawn, preserved, or returned for further governance without destroying its historical continuity.
objects.coreQuestion: When changing information or conditions materially affect a prediction, when must it be preserved, reviewed, revised, superseded, or withdrawn?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Prediction Outcome & Performance Standard (POFPS) governs how a historically identifiable Governed Prediction is associated with a sufficiently governed outcome reference and how predictive performance is subsequently determined, interpreted, compared, calibrated, and preserved without rewriting the prediction, manufacturing certainty after the fact, or confusing favorable outcomes with demonstrated predictive capability.
objects.coreQuestion: Once a sufficiently governed outcome becomes available, how should the prediction be associated with that outcome and its predictive performance legitimately determined over time?

objects.canonicalDefinition: The Prediction Record & Continuity Standard (PRCS) is the Parent Standard within PGA™ that governs how a prediction remains historically identifiable and reconstructable across its complete lifecycle, including every material prediction state, methodological context, Prediction Basis, assumption state, probability and uncertainty representation, formation event, communication state, reliance context, revision, supersession, withdrawal, outcome relationship, performance record, archival state, and subsequent re-entry into active governance.
objects.coreQuestion: How must a prediction and its complete history remain identifiable, reconstructable, versioned, and historically continuous across formation, revision, supersession, outcome, performance assessment, retirement, and lifecycle re-entry?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value Identification Standard (VIS) is the first Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture and governs the methodological conditions under which a potential or existing manifestation of value can be identified, distinguished, bounded, described, and established as a governable Value Object within the value lifecycle.
objects.coreQuestion: What value is being governed, and how can it be sufficiently identified and bounded before its origin, existence, state, and lifecycle are determined?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value Origin Standard (VOS) is the second Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanism and governs the identification, definition, relationship, conditions, and documentation of the origin from which governed value can emerge.

Value Emergence Standard (VES) is the third Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture and governs the conditions under which potential value arising from an identified value origin becomes existent value within a defined Value Context.

Value Recognition Standard (VRS) is the fourth Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governing the conditions under which existing value may be formally recognized as value within a defined governance context.
objects.coreQuestion: When can existing value be recognized as value within its defined governance context?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value State Standard (VSS) is the fifth Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governing the identification, classification, determination, transition readiness, and persistent representation of the current governed state of value.
objects.coreQuestion: What is the current governed state of value?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value Change Standard (VCS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the identification, characterization, magnitude determination, causation linkage, and recording of material change affecting existing governed value.
objects.coreQuestion: When has existing value materially changed, and what change has occurred to it?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value Development Standard (VDS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs how existing value develops positively over time through identifiable growth, maturation, compounding, strengthening, capability expansion, productive improvement, or other forms of governed positive development.
objects.coreQuestion: How does existing value increase, strengthen, mature, compound, or otherwise develop over time?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value Degradation Standard (VDGS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs how existing positive value weakens, declines, deteriorates, erodes, loses capability, loses utility, becomes impaired, or otherwise undergoes progressive negative development while value continues to exist.
objects.coreQuestion: How does existing value weaken, decline, deteriorate, or become progressively impaired while value still exists?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value Nullification Standard (VNS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the conditions, thresholds, mechanisms, determinations, and governed transitions through which previously existing positive value reaches a legitimate zero-value condition.
objects.coreQuestion: When and through what governed transition does existing positive value reach a zero-value condition?

objects.canonicalDefinition: Value Restoration Standard (VRSS) is the tenth Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture governing how previously existing value that has become degraded, impaired, lost, dormant, inaccessible, or zero may legitimately re-emerge as governed value.

Value Extinction Standard (VXSS) is the Parent Standard within VFM® — Value Flow Mechanisms Architecture that governs the terminal lifecycle condition in which previously existing value ceases to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle.
objects.coreQuestion: When does value cease to exist as recoverable value within the governed lifecycle?
